claim: After paralyzing spinal cord injury the adult nervous system has little ability to 'heal' spinal connections.
source: After paralyzing spinal cord injury the adult nervous system has little ability to 'heal' spinal connections, and it is assumed to be unable to develop extra-spinal recovery strategies to bypass the lesion.
evidence: This is a statement about established understanding in the field, drawing from general scientific knowledge about spinal cord injury.

claim: It is assumed that the adult nervous system is unable to develop extra-spinal recovery strategies to bypass the lesion after spinal cord injury.
source: After paralyzing spinal cord injury the adult nervous system has little ability to 'heal' spinal connections, and it is assumed to be unable to develop extra-spinal recovery strategies to bypass the lesion.
evidence: This represents the prevailing assumption in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: Completely spinalized adult rats can recover unassisted hindlimb weight support and locomotion without explicit spinal transmission of motor commands through the lesion.
source: We challenge this assumption, showing that completely spinalized adult rats can recover unassisted hindlimb weight support and locomotion without explicit spinal transmission of motor commands through the lesion.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from behavioral assessments.

claim: Recovery of unassisted hindlimb locomotion is achieved with combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies that maximize cortical reorganization.
source: This is achieved with combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies that maximize cortical reorganization, inducing an expansion of trunk motor cortex and forepaw sensory cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex, associated with sprouting of corticospinal axons.
evidence: This describes the experimental intervention and its effects, supported by the study's experimental design and results.

claim: Combined therapies induce an expansion of trunk motor cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex.
source: This is achieved with combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies that maximize cortical reorganization, inducing an expansion of trunk motor cortex and forepaw sensory cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex, associated with sprouting of corticospinal axons.
evidence: This is supported by motor mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Combined therapies induce an expansion of forepaw sensory cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex.
source: This is achieved with combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies that maximize cortical reorganization, inducing an expansion of trunk motor cortex and forepaw sensory cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex, associated with sprouting of corticospinal axons.
evidence: This is supported by somatosensory mapping data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Combined therapies are associated with sprouting of corticospinal axons.
source: This is achieved with combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies that maximize cortical reorganization, inducing an expansion of trunk motor cortex and forepaw sensory cortex into the deafferented hindlimb cortex, associated with sprouting of corticospinal axons.
evidence: This is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lesioning the reorganized cortex reverses the recovery of hindlimb function.
source: Lesioning the reorganized cortex reverses the recovery.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cortical lesion experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adult rats can develop a novel cortical sensorimotor circuit that bypasses the lesion through biomechanical coupling.
source: Adult rats can thus develop a novel cortical sensorimotor circuit that bypasses the lesion, probably through biomechanical coupling, to partly recover unassisted hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of cortical reorganization data and behavioral recovery, with the biomechanical coupling mechanism being speculative.

claim: Spinal cord injury leads to dramatic loss of motor function below the level of the lesion.
source: Spinal cord injury leads to dramatic loss of motor function below the level of the lesion, often permanently compromising the ability to locomote (van Middendorp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spinal cord injury often permanently compromises the ability to locomote.
source: Spinal cord injury leads to dramatic loss of motor function below the level of the lesion, often permanently compromising the ability to locomote (van Middendorp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury can be achieved by healing the lesion to re-establish motor pathways.
source: From a translational research perspective, recovery of motor function and locomotion can in principle be achieved with at least two conceptually different approaches: (a) 'healing' the lesion to re-establish motor pathways (Richardson et al., 1980; David and Aguayo, 1981); (b) bypassing the lesion to reconnect motor circuits above and below (Ethier et al., 2012; Manohar et al., 2012; Bouton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury can be achieved by bypassing the lesion to reconnect motor circuits above and below.
source: From a translational research perspective, recovery of motor function and locomotion can in principle be achieved with at least two conceptually different approaches: (a) 'healing' the lesion to re-establish motor pathways (Richardson et al., 1980; David and Aguayo, 1981); (b) bypassing the lesion to reconnect motor circuits above and below (Ethier et al., 2012; Manohar et al., 2012; Bouton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The adult spinal cord has limited ability to restore connections through injury.
source: The first approach pursues the regeneration ideal of overcoming the natural limited ability of the adult spinal cord to restore connections through the injury (Selzer, 2003; Liu et al., 2010b; Ruschel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The two approaches to recovery (healing vs bypassing) implicitly assume that the adult nervous system is unable to innately develop a recovery strategy to bypass the lesion.
source: The two approaches – healing vs bypassing the lesion – implicitly assume that the adult nervous system is unable to innately develop a recovery strategy to bypass the lesion.
evidence: This is an inference about the assumptions underlying existing approaches in the field.

claim: Complete thoracic transection in adult rats excludes any spinal transmission of motor commands through the lesion.
source: Specifically: (i) we chose a spinal cord injury model – complete thoracic transection in adult rats – that excludes any spinal transmission of motor commands through the lesion
evidence: This describes the experimental model design and its key property.

claim: Combinations of 5-HT agonists and physical therapies are designed to maximize reorganization of sensorimotor circuits both below and above the level of the lesion.
source: and (ii) we delivered a combination of pharmacological treatment (5-HT agonists) and physical therapies (active treadmill training and/or passive hindlimb bike exercise) designed to maximize reorganization of sensorimotor circuits both below and above the level of the lesion (Courtine et al., 2009; Kao et al., 2009, 2011; Ganzer et al., 2013; Graziano et al., 2013; Oza and Giszter, 2014, 2015; Foffani et al., 2016; Ganzer et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the therapeutic intervention, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maximizing the reorganization of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex creates a novel circuit that responds to input from the ventral forepaws.
source: We show that maximizing the reorganization of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex creates a novel circuit that responds to input from the ventral forepaws and activates trunk muscles that span the lesion.
evidence: This is supported by somatosensory mapping data showing forepaw responses in hindlimb cortex.

claim: Maximizing the reorganization of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex creates a novel circuit that activates trunk muscles that span the lesion.
source: We show that maximizing the reorganization of the hindlimb sensorimotor cortex creates a novel circuit that responds to input from the ventral forepaws and activates trunk muscles that span the lesion.
evidence: This is supported by motor mapping data showing trunk representation expansion.

claim: The new cortical circuit bypasses the lesion via biomechanical coupling.
source: This new cortical circuit bypasses the lesion, probably via biomechanical coupling, allowing animals to recover a surprising level of unassisted hindlimb weight support and locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
evidence: The biomechanical coupling mechanism is speculative, inferred from the anatomical and functional data.

claim: The percentage of weight supported step cycles (%WSS) increased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 4 weeks for animals receiving partial therapy.
source: the %WSS increased by a factor of ten at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 4 weeks both, for animals receiving partial (Tukey: p=0.0644, p=0.0086) and complete therapy (p=0.0300, p=0.0002), but not for transected animals receiving sham therapy (p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The percentage of weight supported step cycles (%WSS) increased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 4 weeks for animals receiving complete therapy.
source: the %WSS increased by a factor of ten at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 4 weeks both, for animals receiving partial (Tukey: p=0.0644, p=0.0086) and complete therapy (p=0.0300, p=0.0002), but not for transected animals receiving sham therapy (p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The percentage of weight supported step cycles (%WSS) did not increase for transected animals receiving sham therapy.
source: the %WSS increased by a factor of ten at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 4 weeks both, for animals receiving partial (Tukey: p=0.0644, p=0.0086) and complete therapy (p=0.0300, p=0.0002), but not for transected animals receiving sham therapy (p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 12 weeks, the %WSS of animals receiving complete therapy (19.4 ± 17.8%) was significantly higher than that of animals that received sham therapy (1.6 ± 2.9%).
source: Moreover, at 12 weeks, the %WSS of animals receiving complete therapy (19.4 ± 17.8%) was significantly higher than that of animals that received sham therapy (1.6 ± 2.9%, p=0.0103) but animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham therapy animals (12.3 ± 15.4%, p=0.32), suggesting that complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 12 weeks, animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham therapy animals in %WSS.
source: Moreover, at 12 weeks, the %WSS of animals receiving complete therapy (19.4 ± 17.8%) was significantly higher than that of animals that received sham therapy (1.6 ± 2.9%, p=0.0103) but animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham therapy animals (12.3 ± 15.4%, p=0.32), suggesting that complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
source: Moreover, at 12 weeks, the %WSS of animals receiving complete therapy (19.4 ± 17.8%) was significantly higher than that of animals that received sham therapy (1.6 ± 2.9%, p=0.0103) but animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham therapy animals (12.3 ± 15.4%, p=0.32), suggesting that complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative behavioral outcomes between therapy groups.

claim: After 12 weeks of complete therapy, three animals were able to perform >40% of WSS.
source: After 12 weeks of complete therapy, three animals were able to perform >40% of WSS (one animal went as high as 56%) during the treadmill session.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data.

claim: One animal achieved 56% WSS after 12 weeks of complete therapy.
source: After 12 weeks of complete therapy, three animals were able to perform >40% of WSS (one animal went as high as 56%) during the treadmill session.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data.

claim: The assisted vertical weight support at load-bearing failure point decreased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks with partial and complete therapy but not with sham therapy.
source: The assisted vertical weight support at load-bearing failure point markedly decreased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks with partial and complete therapy but not with sham therapy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), providing additional direct evidence of increasing levels of hindlimb weight support achieved by the animals.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Open field scores increased at 4 weeks, 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 2 weeks for animals receiving complete therapy.
source: Specifically, open field scores (Basso et al., 1995) were similar across groups at 2 weeks (6.5 ± 1.3 for sham, 5.7 ± 2.0 for partial, 5.2 ± 2.4 for full; 1-way ANOVA, F(2,41)=1.7, p=0.19), and then increased at 4 weeks, 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 2 weeks for animals receiving complete therapy (time x therapy: F(6,123)=3.2, p=0.0064; Tukey: p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of BBB scores shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Open field scores increased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 2 weeks for animals receiving partial therapy.
source: and increased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 2 weeks for animals receiving partial therapy (p<0.0007), but not for transected animals receiving sham therapy (p>0.40).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of BBB scores shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Open field scores did not increase for transected animals receiving sham therapy.
source: and increased at 8 weeks and 12 weeks compared to 2 weeks for animals receiving partial therapy (p<0.0007), but not for transected animals receiving sham therapy (p>0.40).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of BBB scores shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 12 weeks the open field scores of animals that received complete therapy were significantly higher than those of animals that received sham therapy.
source: Again, at 12 weeks the open field scores of animals that received complete therapy were significantly higher than those of animals that received sham therapy (p=0.0137) but animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham (p=0.43), confirming that complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of BBB scores shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 12 weeks, animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham therapy animals in open field scores.
source: Again, at 12 weeks the open field scores of animals that received complete therapy were significantly higher than those of animals that received sham therapy (p=0.0137) but animals that received partial therapy were not different from sham (p=0.43), confirming that complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of BBB scores shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of animals that achieved plantar weight support in the open field increased from <4% at 2 weeks to 47% at 12 weeks with partial or complete therapy.
source: The number of animals that achieved plantar weight support in the open field dramatically increased with partial or complete therapy from <4% at 2 weeks to 47% at 12 weeks, compared to 14% at 12 weeks in animals undergoing sham therapy (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 14% of animals undergoing sham therapy achieved plantar weight support in the open field at 12 weeks.
source: The number of animals that achieved plantar weight support in the open field dramatically increased with partial or complete therapy from <4% at 2 weeks to 47% at 12 weeks, compared to 14% at 12 weeks in animals undergoing sham therapy (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Motor performance during weight-supported treadmill locomotion and open-field motor recovery were highly correlated at 12 weeks after spinal transection (R = 0.60, p<0.0001).
source: Interestingly, 12 weeks after spinal transection motor performance during weight-supported treadmill locomotion and open-field motor recovery were highly correlated (Pearson: R = 0.60, p<0.0001; n = 42; Figure 1D), suggesting that these two measures – quantitative on a treadmill with lateral support and semi-quantitative in the open field – are capturing similar aspects of functional recovery.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treadmill and open field measures are capturing similar aspects of functional recovery.
source: Interestingly, 12 weeks after spinal transection motor performance during weight-supported treadmill locomotion and open-field motor recovery were highly correlated (Pearson: R = 0.60, p<0.0001; n = 42; Figure 1D), suggesting that these two measures – quantitative on a treadmill with lateral support and semi-quantitative in the open field – are capturing similar aspects of functional recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation between the two measures.

claim: The completeness of the spinal lesion was histologically confirmed in all animals with both nissl and 5-HT staining.
source: Importantly, the completeness of the spinal lesion was histologically confirmed in all animals with both nissl and 5-HT staining (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Motor representations of the hindlimbs were absent in all lesioned animals.
source: As expected, motor representations of the hindlimbs – typically observed in naïve intact rats – were absent in all lesioned animals, confirming the completeness of the spinal transection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by motor mapping data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant therapy-dependent reorganization of the deafferented motor cortex.
source: However, there was a significant therapy-dependent reorganization of the deafferented motor cortex (2-way mixed ANOVA, location x therapy: F(4,66)=3.6, p=0.0103; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of motor mapping data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: There was an expansion of the trunk representation in animals that received complete therapy compared to animals that received partial therapy.
source: Specifically, we observed an expansion of the trunk representation in animals that received complete therapy compared to animals that received partial therapy (Tukey, p=0.0484) or sham therapy (p=0.0013).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of motor mapping data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was an expansion of the trunk representation in animals that received complete therapy compared to animals that received sham therapy.
source: Specifically, we observed an expansion of the trunk representation in animals that received complete therapy compared to animals that received partial therapy (Tukey, p=0.0484) or sham therapy (p=0.0013).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of motor mapping data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expansion of trunk representation was not secondary to an increase in cortical excitability.
source: This expansion was not secondary to an in increase in cortical excitability, since there were no differences between the threshold currents across groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by threshold current data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no expansion of the cortical representations of the forelimb into the deafferented motor cortex.
source: We did not observe any expansion of the cortical representations of the forelimb or of the vibrissae into the deafferented motor cortex (p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by motor mapping data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no expansion of the cortical representations of the vibrissae into the deafferented motor cortex.
source: We did not observe any expansion of the cortical representations of the forelimb or of the vibrissae into the deafferented motor cortex (p>0.99).
evidence: This is supported by motor mapping data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cortical area of the trunk representation correlated with motor performance measured by %WSS (R = 0.41, p=0.0142).
source: Importantly, considering all animals, the cortical area of the trunk representation correlated with motor performance, measured by both %WSS (Pearson: R = 0.41, p=0.0142; n = 36; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cortical area of the trunk representation correlated with motor performance measured by open field scores (R = 0.51, p=0.0013).
source: and open field scores (Pearson: R = 0.51, p=0.0013; n = 36; Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Lesioning the reorganized motor cortex dramatically decreased the motor performance as measured by %WSS during treadmill locomotion.
source: Lesioning the reorganized motor cortex dramatically decreased the motor performance as measured by %WSS during treadmill locomotion (2-way ANOVA, lesion: F(1,20)=24.0, p<0.0001; lesion x therapy: F(1,20)=0.1, p=0.70; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data after cortical lesion shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ability to make plantar contact with the treadmill during stepping differentiates animals that achieved good recovery from animals that displayed poor recovery.
source: The key element that differentiated animals that achieved good recovery from animals that displayed poor recovery was the ability to make plantar contact with the treadmill during stepping, which was lost after the cortical lesion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by video analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability to make plantar contact with the treadmill during stepping was lost after the cortical lesion.
source: The key element that differentiated animals that achieved good recovery from animals that displayed poor recovery was the ability to make plantar contact with the treadmill during stepping, which was lost after the cortical lesion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by video analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cortical lesion decreased the number of animals that achieved plantar weight support in the open field from 47% at week-12 to 36% and 27% after the cortical lesion in animals under partial or complete therapy, respectively.
source: In agreement, the cortical lesion also decreased the number of animals that achieved plantar weight support in the open field (BBB ≥ 9) from 47% at week-12, to 36% and 27% after the cortical lesion in animals under partial or complete therapy, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by BBB score data after cortical lesion shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The %WSS for the forelimbs was 100% for all animals at week-12 and remained 100% for all animals at week-14, after the cortical lesion.
source: The %WSS for the forelimbs was 100% for all animals at week-12 and remained 100% for all animals at week-14, after the cortical lesion.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data.

claim: 100% of forelimb steps were plantar steps both before and after the cortical lesion.
source: Furthermore, 100% of forelimb steps were plantar steps both before and after the cortical lesion.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the behavioral data.

claim: Forelimb weight support remained unobstructed by the cortical lesion.
source: Forelimb weight support thus remained unobstructed by the cortical lesion, supporting the specificity of the cortical lesion to hindlimb function.
evidence: This is inferred from the forelimb behavioral data before and after cortical lesion.

claim: The cortical lesion was specific to hindlimb function.
source: Forelimb weight support thus remained unobstructed by the cortical lesion, supporting the specificity of the cortical lesion to hindlimb function.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on hindlimb vs forelimb function.

claim: The same cortical lesion performed in naïve intact animals did not induce any change in motor performance either on the treadmill or in the open field.
source: As a control, the same cortical lesion performed in a group of naïve intact animals (n = 4) did not induce any change in motor performance either on the treadmill or in the open field (100%WSS and BBB = 21 both before and after the cortical lesion).
evidence: This is a direct observation from control experiments.

claim: The reorganization of the motor cortex is at least partly responsible for the hindlimb motor recovery after complete spinal cord transection.
source: These results suggest that the reorganization of the motor cortex is at least partly responsible for the hindlimb motor recovery after complete spinal cord transection.
evidence: This is inferred from the cortical lesion experiments showing reversal of recovery.

claim: There was a rostro-caudal gradient of axonal innervation from the hindlimb motor cortex into the spinal cord.
source: There was a rostro-caudal gradient of axonal innervation from the hindlimb motor cortex into the spinal cord (two-way ANOVA, level: F(2,81)=7.3, p=0.0012), with more counts at T7 level compared to T4 (Tukey, p=0.0054) and T1 (p=0.0030).
evidence: This is supported by axon counting data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: Therapy after spinal cord transection promoted corticospinal sprouting.
source: More importantly, therapy after spinal cord transection promoted corticospinal sprouting (therapy, F(2,81)=6.4, p=0.0027).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of axon counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: More axons were counted in the gray matter of the thoracic spinal cord in transected animals that underwent complete therapy compared to transected animals that underwent sham therapy.
source: Specifically, more axons were counted in the gray matter of the thoracic spinal cord in transected animals that underwent complete therapy compared to both transected animals that underwent sham therapy (p=0.0111) and naïve intact animals (p=0.0055) (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of axon counting data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: More axons were counted in the gray matter of the thoracic spinal cord in transected animals that underwent complete therapy compared to naïve intact animals.
source: Specifically, more axons were counted in the gray matter of the thoracic spinal cord in transected animals that underwent complete therapy compared to both transected animals that underwent sham therapy (p=0.0111) and naïve intact animals (p=0.0055) (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of axon counting data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Corticospinal sprouting originating in the deafferented hindlimb cortex into the gray matter of the spinal cord above the level of the lesion could allow animals to gain greater control of trunk musculature.
source: These results show that our therapy regimen promotes sprouting of corticospinal fibers, originating in the deafferented hindlimb cortex, into the gray matter of the spinal cord above the level of the lesion. This corticospinal sprouting could allow animals to gain greater control of trunk musculature, thus contributing to the observed motor recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical location of the sprouting and its potential functional consequences.

claim: Neurons in the hindlimb cortex did not have significant responses to trunk stimulation either before or after spinal cord injury.
source: Note that neurons in the hindlimb cortex did not have significant responses to trunk stimulation either before or after spinal cord injury, likely because the trunk sensory area is not topographically adjacent to the deafferented hindlimb region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from somatosensory mapping experiments.

claim: The trunk sensory area is not topographically adjacent to the deafferented hindlimb region.
source: Note that neurons in the hindlimb cortex did not have significant responses to trunk stimulation either before or after spinal cord injury, likely because the trunk sensory area is not topographically adjacent to the deafferented hindlimb region.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cortical topography.

claim: The percentage of responding cells was highly dependent on whether transected animals received complete or sham therapy.
source: However, the percentage of responding cells was highly dependent on whether transected animals received complete or sham therapy (two-way GZLM, therapy x time, Wald χ2(3)=12.7, p=0.0054).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of somatosensory mapping data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The percentage of responding cells became significantly higher in animals that received complete therapy compared to sham therapy at week 4, week 8 and week 12 after spinal cord transection.
source: Namely, even though the two groups were expectedly not different at week zero before the spinal transection (Tukey, p=0.42), the percentage of responding cells became significantly higher in animals that received complete therapy compared to sham therapy at week 4 (p=0.0128), week 8 (p<0.0001) and week 12 (p<0.0001) after spinal cord transection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of somatosensory mapping data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In animals that received complete therapy after spinal cord transection, the probability to record responsive cells expanded toward more medial and more rostral electrodes.
source: We found that in animals that received complete therapy after spinal cord transection, the probability to record responsive cells expanded toward more medial and more rostral electrodes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis of somatosensory mapping data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The response magnitude specifically increased in the medial-rostral quadrant of the array (Q2) but not in the other quadrants.
source: In fact, the response magnitude (spikes/stimulus) of the recorded cells specifically increased in the medial-rostral quadrant of the array (Q2; t-test, p=0.002; bonferroni-corrected alpha = 0.0125) but not in the other quadrants (p>0.118; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of response magnitude data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The medial-rostral expansion of the forelimb somatosensory representation overlaps with the expanded trunk motor representation.
source: This medial-rostral expansion of the forelimb somatosensory representation nicely overlaps with the expanded trunk motor representation we described above, suggesting that integrated sensorimotor cortical reorganization is likely to contribute to the motor recovery induced by therapy after spinal cord transection (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the spatial patterns of motor and sensory reorganization shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Integrated sensorimotor cortical reorganization is likely to contribute to the motor recovery induced by therapy after spinal cord transection.
source: This medial-rostral expansion of the forelimb somatosensory representation nicely overlaps with the expanded trunk motor representation we described above, suggesting that integrated sensorimotor cortical reorganization is likely to contribute to the motor recovery induced by therapy after spinal cord transection (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap of sensory and motor reorganization.

claim: Neurons in the hindlimb cortex were responsive to forepaw placement during normal treadmill locomotion.
source: Importantly, neurons in the hindlimb cortex were responsive to forepaw placement during normal treadmill locomotion, with their peak response latency being distributed across a broad range of phases in the locomotion cycle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from awake recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peak response latency of neurons in the hindlimb cortex to forepaw placement was distributed across a broad range of phases in the locomotion cycle.
source: Importantly, neurons in the hindlimb cortex were responsive to forepaw placement during normal treadmill locomotion, with their peak response latency being distributed across a broad range of phases in the locomotion cycle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from awake recordings shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Broad normal responsiveness of hindlimb cortex neurons to forepaw placement provides a possible functional substrate for cortical reorganization after spinal cord injury.
source: This broad normal responsiveness provides a possible functional substrate for the cortical reorganization after spinal cord injury
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of broad responsiveness in normal animals.

claim: Previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats using sensorimotor rehabilitation.
source: Several previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats, either using sensorimotor rehabilitation(de Leon et al., 2002; Alluin et al., 2015), administration of serotonergic agonists (Feraboli-Lohnherr et al., 1999; Antri et al., 2002, Antri et al., 2005), transplants below the level of the lesion (Giménez Y Ribotta et al., 2000, Sławińska et al., 2013) or combined pharmacological and electrical stimulation (Gerasimenko et al., 2007; Ichiyama et al., 2008; Courtine et al., 2009; Musienko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats using administration of serotonergic agonists.
source: Several previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats, either using sensorimotor rehabilitation(de Leon et al., 2002; Alluin et al., 2015), administration of serotonergic agonists (Feraboli-Lohnherr et al., 1999; Antri et al., 2002, Antri et al., 2005), transplants below the level of the lesion (Giménez Y Ribotta et al., 2000, Sławińska et al., 2013) or combined pharmacological and electrical stimulation (Gerasimenko et al., 2007; Ichiyama et al., 2008; Courtine et al., 2009; Musienko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats using transplants below the level of the lesion.
source: Several previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats, either using sensorimotor rehabilitation(de Leon et al., 2002; Alluin et al., 2015), administration of serotonergic agonists (Feraboli-Lohnherr et al., 1999; Antri et al., 2002, Antri et al., 2005), transplants below the level of the lesion (Giménez Y Ribotta et al., 2000, Sławińska et al., 2013) or combined pharmacological and electrical stimulation (Gerasimenko et al., 2007; Ichiyama et al., 2008; Courtine et al., 2009; Musienko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats using combined pharmacological and electrical stimulation.
source: Several previous studies were able to improve hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats, either using sensorimotor rehabilitation(de Leon et al., 2002; Alluin et al., 2015), administration of serotonergic agonists (Feraboli-Lohnherr et al., 1999; Antri et al., 2002, Antri et al., 2005), transplants below the level of the lesion (Giménez Y Ribotta et al., 2000, Sławińska et al., 2013) or combined pharmacological and electrical stimulation (Gerasimenko et al., 2007; Ichiyama et al., 2008; Courtine et al., 2009; Musienko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All previous interventions required either tail pinching, perineal stimulation and/or some level of assisted vertical weight support to achieve hindlimb locomotion in adult spinalized rats.
source: However, all previous interventions required either tail pinching, perineal stimulation and/or some level of assisted vertical weight support to achieve hindlimb locomotion in adult spinalized rats.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of previous studies in the field.

claim: During treadmill testing and open-field evaluation, animals in this study received no form of peripheral stimulation or assisted vertical weight support.
source: In our study, during treadmill testing and open-field evaluation our animals received no form of peripheral stimulation or assisted vertical weight support.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions of the current study.

claim: No movement could be elicited below the level of the lesion by microstimulation of the hindlimb motor cortex.
source: Apart from improbable regeneration across the lesion, the immediate most logical explanation is to think about residual connections (Waxman, 1989; Courtine et al., 2008; Cowley et al., 2010; Flynn et al., 2011; Zaporozhets et al., 2011; Shah et al., 2013; Filli et al., 2014), but this possibility is excluded by both physiological and anatomical evidence in our experiments: (a) no movement whatsoever could be elicited below the level of the lesion by microstimulation of the hindlimb motor cortex
evidence: This is a direct observation from motor mapping experiments.

claim: Trunk muscles extend from above to below the level of the injury.
source: An alternative explanation is suggested by the functional expansion of the trunk cortical representation. Trunk muscles do extend from above to below the level of the injury, thus providing a biomechanical substrate for bypassing the lesion.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of trunk musculature.

claim: Treated animals learned to activate the trunk musculature to reduce the load on the hindlimbs while balancing on the forelimbs, which allowed the central-pattern-generators below the level of the lesion to be activated.
source: The idea is that our treated animals learned to activate the trunk musculature to reduce the load on the hindlimbs while balancing on the forelimbs, which allowed the central-pattern-generators below the level of the lesion to be activated, resulting in weight-supported hindlimb stepping.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Neonatally spinalized rats can develop unassisted weight-supported stepping.
source: This explanation is supported by previous observations in neonatally spinalized rats (Giszter et al., 2007, 2008, 2010), which can develop unassisted weight-supported stepping (Stelzner et al., 1975; Weber and Stelzner, 1977; Commissiong and Sauve, 1993; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The motor recovery of neonatally spinalized rats is not due to any reconnection within the spinal cord.
source: Importantly, the motor recovery of neonatally spinalized rats is not due to any reconnection within the spinal cord (Cummings et al., 1981; Tillakaratne et al., 2010), but is instead causally related to sensorimotor cortical reorganization (Giszter et al., 1998, 2008; Kao et al., 2009, 2011; Moxon et al., 2013; Oza and Giszter, 2015; Udoekwere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The motor recovery of neonatally spinalized rats is causally related to sensorimotor cortical reorganization.
source: Importantly, the motor recovery of neonatally spinalized rats is not due to any reconnection within the spinal cord (Cummings et al., 1981; Tillakaratne et al., 2010), but is instead causally related to sensorimotor cortical reorganization (Giszter et al., 1998, 2008; Kao et al., 2009, 2011; Moxon et al., 2013; Oza and Giszter, 2015; Udoekwere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recovery of unassisted weight-supported hindlimb stepping after complete spinal cord injury was believed to remain restricted to neonatally spinalized rats, due to the higher cortical plasticity at neonatal age compared to adulthood.
source: Until now, recovery of unassisted weight-supported hindlimb stepping after complete spinal cord injury was believed to remain restricted to neonatally spinalized rats, due to the higher cortical plasticity at neonatal age compared to adulthood (Oza and Giszter, 2015; Udoekwere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Carefully designed combinations of pharmaceutical and physical therapies after spinal cord transection can produce sufficient cortical plasticity to recover unassisted weight supported hindlimb stepping after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats.
source: Our results show that carefully designed combinations of pharmaceutical and physical therapies after spinal cord transection can produce sufficient cortical plasticity to recover unassisted weight supported hindlimb stepping after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The overlap of sensorimotor reorganization unifies previous studies on somatosensory or motor reorganization into a joint framework.
source: This overlap of sensorimotor reorganization unifies previous studies on somatosensory (Endo et al., 2007; Kao et al., 2009; Ghosh et al., 2010; Ganzer et al., 2013; Graziano et al., 2013; Humanes-Valera et al., 2017) or motor (Fouad et al., 2001; Giszter et al., 2008; van den Brand et al., 2012; Oza and Giszter, 2014, 2015; Ganzer et al., 2016) reorganization into a joint framework, and is likely to be a key factor for the observed functional recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the current results in the context of previous literature.

claim: The overlap of sensorimotor reorganization is likely to be a key factor for the observed functional recovery.
source: This overlap of sensorimotor reorganization unifies previous studies on somatosensory (Endo et al., 2007; Kao et al., 2009; Ghosh et al., 2010; Ganzer et al., 2013; Graziano et al., 2013; Humanes-Valera et al., 2017) or motor (Fouad et al., 2001; Giszter et al., 2008; van den Brand et al., 2012; Oza and Giszter, 2014, 2015; Ganzer et al., 2016) reorganization into a joint framework, and is likely to be a key factor for the observed functional recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between sensorimotor reorganization and behavioral recovery.

claim: Lesioning the reorganized cortex reversed the recovery of hindlimb function without affecting forelimb function.
source: Indeed, lesioning the reorganized cortex reversed the recovery of hindlimb function, without affecting forelimb function.
evidence: This is supported by data from cortical lesion experiments.

claim: The cortical lesion did not produce any evident functional impairment in naïve non-spinal-cord-injured animals.
source: Intriguingly, our cortical lesion did not produce any evident functional impairment in naïve non-spinal-cord-injured animals, in agreement with recent data suggesting that motor cortex is required for learning but not for executing a learned motor skill in normal rats (Kawai et al., 2015) and with the view that in rodents the motor cortex is not required for normal locomotion (Courtine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments and citations to previous literature.

claim: Motor cortex is required for learning but not for executing a learned motor skill in normal rats.
source: Intriguingly, our cortical lesion did not produce any evident functional impairment in naïve non-spinal-cord-injured animals, in agreement with recent data suggesting that motor cortex is required for learning but not for executing a learned motor skill in normal rats (Kawai et al., 2015) and with the view that in rodents the motor cortex is not required for normal locomotion (Courtine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In rodents the motor cortex is not required for normal locomotion.
source: Intriguingly, our cortical lesion did not produce any evident functional impairment in naïve non-spinal-cord-injured animals, in agreement with recent data suggesting that motor cortex is required for learning but not for executing a learned motor skill in normal rats (Kawai et al., 2015) and with the view that in rodents the motor cortex is not required for normal locomotion (Courtine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The motor cortex is required to sustain the recovered locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
source: Crucially, our data suggest that the motor cortex is indeed required to sustain the recovered locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the cortical lesion experiments showing reversal of recovery.

claim: Combinations of therapies after spinal cord injury might be able to rescue at least some features of critical period plasticity.
source: In any case, the relationship between cortical plasticity and functional recovery in our adult spinalized rats is very similar to neonatally spinalized rats, suggesting that combinations of therapies after spinal cord injury might be able to rescue at least some features of critical period plasticity (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008; Murphy and Corbett, 2009; Yamahachi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between adult and neonatal recovery patterns, with support from citations.

claim: Cortico-spinal sprouting is in agreement with many previous studies in several models of spinal cord injury.
source: This cortico-spinal sprouting is in agreement with many previous studies in several models of spinal cord injury (Fouad et al., 2001; Weidner et al., 2001; Bareyre et al., 2004; Barritt et al., 2006; Vavrek et al., 2006; Girgis et al., 2007; García-Alías et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2009; Ghosh et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011; Floriddia et al., 2012; Scali et al., 2013; Du et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Subcortical plasticity is likely to have contributed to the observed functional recovery.
source: Overall, even though subcortical plasticity is likely to have contributed to the observed functional recovery (Kambi et al., 2014; Alonso-Calviño et al., 2016), our results suggest that at least part of the plasticity induced by our therapies after spinal cord injury is genuinely cortical.
evidence: This is inferred from general knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: At least part of the plasticity induced by therapies after spinal cord injury is genuinely cortical.
source: Overall, even though subcortical plasticity is likely to have contributed to the observed functional recovery (Kambi et al., 2014; Alonso-Calviño et al., 2016), our results suggest that at least part of the plasticity induced by our therapies after spinal cord injury is genuinely cortical.
evidence: This is inferred from the cortical mapping and lesion data.

claim: The novel cortical sensorimotor circuit developed in rats integrates sensory information from the ventral forepaws and motor control to the muscles of the spine.
source: Indeed, the novel cortical sensorimotor circuit developed in our rats – integrating sensory information from the ventral forepaws and motor control to the muscles of the spine – suggests that the closed-loop control of trunk musculature that is sufficient for quadrupedal functional improvement might be irrelevant for bipedal locomotion.
evidence: This is inferred from the sensory and motor mapping data.

claim: Patients attempting to recover locomotion after a spinal cord injury make significant use of the upper limbs to handle their walking aids, so that locomotion behavior switches from the normal bipedal pattern to an assisted quasi-quadrupedal pattern.
source: However, it can be argued that patients attempting to recover locomotion after a spinal cord injury make significant use of the upper limbs to handle their walking aids, so that locomotion behavior switches from the normal bipedal pattern to an assisted quasi-quadrupedal pattern (Del-Ama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Supraspinal control of trunk stability might become critical to achieve locomotion in recovering patients with spinal cord injury.
source: From this quasi-quadrupedal perspective, this novel supraspinal control of trunk stability – with possible involvement of intersegmental reflexes (Tani et al., 1997) – might become critical to achieve locomotion in recovering patients with spinal cord injury, as in our animals.
evidence: This is speculative, inferred from the animal results and supported by a citation.

claim: Therapeutic interventions after spinal cord injury can act at multiple levels of the sensorimotor system.
source: However, therapeutic interventions after spinal cord injury can act at multiple levels of the sensorimotor system (Onifer et al., 2011; Musienko et al., 2012; van den Brand et al., 2012), including the skeletomuscular system (Hangartner et al., 1994; Lauer et al., 2011), muscular-spinal reflex circuits (Mello et al., 2004; Hamid and Hayek, 2008; Phadke et al., 2009; Rayegani et al., 2011), and neural circuits within the spinal cord (Liu et al., 2010a; Côté et al., 2011; Keeler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When combined together, different therapies can have redundant or synergistic effects on cortical plasticity and recovery.
source: Consequently, when combined together, different therapies can have redundant or synergistic effects on cortical plasticity and recovery (Foffani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Well-designed combinations of therapies should be employed to maximize corticospinal plasticity and functional outcome.
source: The present results support the view that well-designed combinations of therapies should be employed to maximize corticospinal plasticity and functional outcome (Thuret et al., 2006; Hollis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the current results and supported by citations.

claim: This study substantially raises the standard of behavioral recovery that adult rats can achieve after a spinal cord injury without any spinal transmission of signals through the lesioned cord.
source: Finally, our study substantially raises the standard of behavioral recovery that adult rats can achieve after a spinal cord injury without any spinal transmission of signals through the lesioned cord (and without any external support or sensory stimulation).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current results to previous literature.

claim: Any work attempting to restore sensorimotor communication through the lesion after spinal cord injury should carefully consider the possibility that at least part of the functional recovery might be unrelated to the restored spinal communication.
source: Any work attempting to restore sensorimotor communication through the lesion after spinal cord injury should carefully consider the possibility that at least part of the functional recovery might be unrelated to the restored spinal communication.
evidence: This is a recommendation inferred from the current findings.

claim: Careful combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies in adult rats can create a novel cortical sensorimotor circuit that is able to bypass the lesion through biomechanical coupling to partly recover unassisted hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
source: Overall, our results show that careful combinations of pharmacological and physical therapies in adult rats can create a novel cortical sensorimotor circuit that is able to bypass the lesion – probably through biomechanical coupling – to partly recover unassisted hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: It is important to take advantage of plasticity along the entire neural axis when developing therapies to optimize recovery of function after severe spinal cord injury.
source: These results demonstrate the importance of taking advantage of plasticity along the entire neural axis when developing therapies to optimize recovery of function after severe spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a recommendation inferred from the current findings.

claim: A total of 74 adult female Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 250–300 g were used in this study.
source: A total of 74 adult female Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 250–300 g were used in this study, divided in three sets of experiments: 54 for experiment 1 (behavioral assessment followed by motor mapping followed by cortical lesioning), 6 for experiment 2 (tract tracing) and 14 for experiment 3 (somatosensory maps).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: The percentage of plantar steps was markedly higher in performers and significantly decreased after the lesion in performers but not in non-performers.
source: Finally, the percentage of plantar steps was markedly higher in performers (group: F(1,40)=95.7, p<0.0001) and significantly decreased after the lesion in performers (lesion x group: F(1,40)=19.9, p<0.0001; Tukey: p=0.0002) but not in non-performers (Tukey: p=0.11).
evidence: This is supported by video analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
